"executive_summary": "This study addresses the challenge of decoding dynamic brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data, where the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response exhibits inherent latency and temporal dynamics. Conventional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models typically only utilize past temporal context, which may be insufficient for capturing the full dynamics of the BOLD signal without manual delay adjustments. The authors propose a Bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) architecture that simultaneously encodes information from both past and future time instances. By collating forward and reverse hidden activations, the model explicitly models BOLD response dynamics without requiring hard-coded delay adjustments. The study utilizes working memory task data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), involving 400 participants performing a 2-back task. The bi-LSTM model was compared against a unidirectional LSTM and a feed-forward neural network. Results demonstrate that the bi-LSTM approach significantly outperforms the unidirectional counterpart, achieving an accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18, representing an 18% improvement. The study concludes that future temporal context is crucial for robust brain state decoding and that the proposed method offers a more natural way to handle BOLD latency.",

summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal; Priya Aggarwal; Luiz Pessoa; Anubha Gupta
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the challenge of decoding dynamic brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data, where the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response exhibits inherent latency and temporal dynamics. Conventional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models typically only utilize past temporal context, which may be insufficient for capturing the full dynamics of the BOLD signal without manual delay adjustments. The authors propose a Bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) architecture that simultaneously encodes information from both past and future time instances. By collating forward and reverse hidden activations, the model explicitly models BOLD response dynamics without requiring hard-coded delay adjustments. The study utilizes working memory task data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), involving 400 participants performing a 2-back task. The bi-LSTM model was compared against a unidirectional LSTM and a feed-forward neural network. Results demonstrate that the bi-LSTM approach significantly outperforms the unidirectional counterpart, achieving an accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18, representing an 18% improvement. The study concludes that future temporal context is crucial for robust brain state decoding and that the proposed method offers a more natural way to handle BOLD latency.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the challenge of decoding dynamic brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data, where the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response exhibits inherent latency and temporal dynamics. Conventional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models typically only utilize past temporal context, which may be insufficient for capturing the full dynamics of the BOLD signal without manual delay adjustments. The authors propose a Bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) architecture that simultaneously encodes information from both past and future time instances. By collating forward and reverse hidden activations, the model explicitly models BOLD response dynamics without requiring hard-coded delay adjustments. The study utilizes working memory task data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), involving 400 participants performing a 2-back task. The bi-LSTM model was compared against a unidirectional LSTM and a feed-forward neural network. Results demonstrate that the bi-LSTM approach significantly outperforms the unidirectional counterpart, achieving an accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18, representing an 18% improvement. The study concludes that future temporal context is crucial for robust brain state decoding and that the proposed method offers a more natural way to handle BOLD latency.

Research Context
Decoding brain states via discriminative feature representations has gained significant interest in brain imaging studies. There is an impetus to encode the dynamics of brain functioning by analyzing temporal information available in the fMRI data. Long-short term memory (LSTM) models are increasingly observed to perform well in applications with dynamic temporal behavior. Conventional decoding methods involved massive univariate analysis measuring activity from thousands of brain locations separately. Multivariate analysis helps in integrating distributed but overlapping information across the spatial domain. Due to the time-lag observed in the peak of BOLD response, it is typically not considered to be synchronized with stimuli. Before training models, each time point is adjusted according to the estimated delay of the BOLD signal. Recent fMRI studies have used LSTM networks for integrating temporal information from the past. Variations in latency of BOLD responses across time suggest that future temporal context is also important.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to perform robust brain state decoding via information encapsulation from both past and future instances of fMRI data. The hypothesis is that bi-directional LSTM allows for explicitly modeling the dynamics of BOLD response without any delay adjustment. The two hidden activations of forward and reverse directions in bi-LSTM are collated to build the memory of the model. The model is expected to robustly predict the brain states at every time instance using this collated memory. The performance of the bi-LSTM network is compared with its conventional unidirectional counterpart in brain state decoding. This framework does not require any time-delay adjustment for the synchronization of stimuli and BOLD response. It is hypothesized that the bi-LSTM will outperform the unidirectional LSTM in terms of accuracy. The study evaluates this method for predicting brain states in working memory fMRI data obtained from the Human Connectome Project.

Methodological Details
The study evaluated the bi-LSTM framework on task fMRI data of the working memory from Human Connectome Project. Participants performed a working memory task indicating if the current stimulus matches with the one presented two stimuli before. The task is called the 2-back task, or a control condition called the 0-back. Participants were presented with separate blocks of trials consisting of 4 different types of stimuli. The stimuli categories are tools, places, faces, and body parts, separated with the fixation period. Data for two runs is available for each participant in the dataset. Within each run, there were 8 task blocks for every task and stimuli combination. Each task block lasted for 27.5 seconds with 4 fixation blocks of 15 seconds each. Each scan is a 405 time-points long sequence of fMRI volumes. The available preprocessed data contains field-map based distortion correction and functional to structural alignment. Motion-related variables were regressed-out using the 3dDeconvolve with ortvec option in the AFNI software. Changes in low frequency signals were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve routine with the polort option. The study used only the cortical data, which is directly available in surface representation. The parcellation method collates the individual voxels within each region by averaging. The method generates 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs). The region-averaged timeseries was used as the input feature vector for the temporal analysis. The generated 405 time-points sequence of 360 ROIs were structured in a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed to adjust for delay in the BOLD response. Each time-point in task blocks was marked as present in one of the above mentioned brain-states. Time instants belonging to the fixation blocks were labelled as others. This yields a total of S = 9 brain states in the classification task.

Procedures And Architectures
Brain-state decoding is essentially modelled as the task of classifying the brain state. The LSTM defines gated cells that can act on the received input activation by passing or blocking information. The learning process is called Backpropagation through time (BPTT). The transition equations for a LSTM model define the output of forget gate, input gate, cell activation, and hidden activation. A schematic illustration of Bidirectional LSTM is provided in Fig. 1. It processes the time-series data in both the directions using separate hidden layers. It computes the forward hidden activation using the standard LSTM equations. The backward hidden activation is calculated by using the future temporal dependency. The input to the subsequent layer is generated by combining both forward and backward hidden activations. The three possible ways of combining the activations are vector concatenation, element-wise vector addition, and element-wise averaging. The input activations to the layer are extracted from the 360 brain ROIs. The last layer of bi-LSTM is followed by a fully-connected layer having S neurons and softmax activation. The bi-LSTM architecture with the same specifications as in previous work was built for comparison. At any given time t, input activations pass through two hidden bi-LSTM layers. Each LSTM cell has 256 hidden activations to encode the temporal dependencies. This is followed by a fully-connected layer containing S = 9 neurons predicting the brain states. The study employed inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation. Data from N = 400 participants was divided into 10 parts for validation. The development set was randomly shuffled and split into 80-20 training-validation sets. The full-length training data was windowed into small overlapping sizes with the window size w = 40. The window had an overlap of 10 points. The proposed model was implemented in Keras deep learning framework. The model was trained on GeForce GTX 980 GPU with a batch size of 32. The optimizer used was ADAM with a learning rate of 0.001. The model was trained for 100 epochs and no early stopping was performed. A dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers for training to prevent over-fitting. Weights for the imbalanced classes were estimated using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine. The model was compared with a three layer feed-forward Neural Network (ff-NN).

Key Results
The overall accuracy of the unidirectional LSTM model was 0.66 ± 0.18. The classification accuracy of the bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM-c) was 0.84 ± 0.02. The bi-LSTM-c model performed 18% better than its unidirectional counterpart in terms of accuracy. For every brain-state, the LSTM model miss-classify to a larger extent compared to the bi-LSTM-c model. The misclassification is highest for both the models to the Others class. The second highest confusion occurs when participants were stimulated with faces and places. The model also gets confused between the stimuli body and tools. The mean normalised confusion matrices on the classification accuracy are illustrated in Fig. 2. The miss-classifications of both LSTM and bi-LSTM-c are compared in Fig. 2. The bi-LSTM architecture demonstrated superior performance compared to the unidirectional LSTM. The model works well without any hard-coded delay adjustment. The problem of class imbalance, although majorly handled, still requires more sophisticated handling. It would be interesting to study about cortical regions engaged in stimuli body and tools.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study proposes to use Bi-directional LSTM network model for decoding brain states from task fMRI data. The goal is to appropriately capture the dynamics of fMRI BOLD response. The experimental results demonstrated superior performance of Bi-LSTM compared to the unidirectional LSTM. This model works well without any hard-coded delay adjustment. The results emphasize the availability of useful information in the immediate future samples as well. The study worked with the fixed window length for time-series chunking. Future work may involve tuning the window-size and overlap for time-series chunking. The problem of class imbalance, although majorly handled, still requires more sophisticated handling. It would be interesting to study about cortical regions engaged in stimuli body and tools. The availability of useful information in the immediate future samples is crucial for accurate decoding. The bi-LSTM framework explicitly models the dynamics of BOLD response without delay adjustment. The collation of forward and backward hidden activations builds the memory of the model.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study worked with the fixed window length, although future work may involve tuning the window-size. The problem of class imbalance, although majorly handled, still requires more sophisticated handling. The model sometimes gets confused between the stimuli body and tools. It would be interesting to study about cortical regions engaged in stimuli body and tools. The study used only the cortical data, which is directly available in surface representation. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed to adjust for delay in the BOLD response. The number of time-instances of class others in the data were much more than any other class. The study did not perform early stopping during training. The study utilized data from the Human Connectome Project which may have specific demographic constraints. The comparison was limited to specific architectures like ff-NN and unidirectional LSTM.

Claims
Bidirectional LSTM significantly outperforms unidirectional LSTM in decoding brain states from fMRI data. The overall accuracy of the unidirectional LSTM model was 0.66 ± 0.18. The classification accuracy of the bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM-c) was 0.84 ± 0.02. The bi-LSTM-c model performed 18% better than its unidirectional counterpart in terms of accuracy. The misclassification is highest for both the models to the Others class. This model works well without any hard-coded delay adjustment.
Future temporal context is crucial for capturing the dynamics of BOLD response. Because of the dynamics and inherent latency in fMRI BOLD responses, future temporal context is crucial. The two hidden activations of forward and reverse directions in bi-LSTM are collated to build the memory of the model. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed to adjust for delay in the BOLD response. This framework does not require any time-delay adjustment for the synchronization of stimuli and BOLD response.

Data And Code Availability
More details about fMRI data acquisition and task paradigm are available at the Human Connectome Project. The proposed model was implemented in Keras deep learning framework.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model was compared with a three layer feed-forward Neural Network (ff-NN). For better comparison, the number of layers and the number of neural units in the layers for the other models were kept same. The study employed inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation. The validation data was generated to tune the hyperparameters and to prevent over-fitting. A dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers for training. Weights for the imbalanced classes were estimated using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine.

Ethical Considerations
The study utilized working memory data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). Participants performed a working memory task indicating if the current stimulus matches with the one presented two stimuli before.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the use of Bi-directional LSTM for decoding brain states without delay adjustment. 2. The strongest evidence is the 18% improvement in accuracy over unidirectional LSTM. 3. The future path involves tuning window-size and overlap and studying cortical regions for body and tools.
